title: Charismatic renewal (1967)
hookLine: a movement of praise and gifts of the Spirit that began at a student retreat

lines: INTO THE CHAPEL, ONE BY ONE.
cards: A weekend retreat house outside Pittsburgh. College students from Duquesne University have come to pray, reading the opening chapters of the Acts of the Apostles: the wind and the fire at Pentecost.

Their question is simple and a little dangerous: could that still happen? By the movement's own telling, on the Saturday night some of them wandered into the chapel, one by one, and didn't come out for a long time.
They prayed, they praised; some wept, some laughed. Nobody had planned it. Out of that weekend, people say, a movement spread through the Catholic Church.

teach.h: PENTECOST: FILLED WITH THE HOLY GHOST.
teach.b: Start with the page they were reading. At Pentecost, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they began to speak with divers tongues, according as the Holy Ghost gave them to speak."
The renewal takes that as more than a memory. Its members pray, in their own words, for the Spirit to stir up what was already given in baptism and confirmation.
They call it being baptized in the Spirit, and they're careful to say it isn't a new sacrament.

The name comes from charisms, the gifts of grace Paul lists for Corinth: wisdom, knowledge, healing, prophecy, tongues and more. And he insists, "Now there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit."
The Catechism takes Paul's line: charisms are graces given for building up the Church, to be received with gratitude and tested by the Church's pastors. What does it look like?

teach.h: A PRAYER MEETING IN A PARISH HALL.
teach.b: A prayer meeting in a parish hall. Songs of praise, some hands raised, a reading, a long stretch of people praising God aloud in their own words, sometimes praying in tongues, then quiet. For some Catholics this is home.
Others pray in silence and find it strange. Both are in the same Church.
And Paul set a guardrail for an enthusiastic church: "Let all things be done decently, and according to order." Praise, with the Church's order around it.

teach.h: DIVERSITIES OF GRACES, BUT THE SAME SPIRIT.
teach.b: One short line runs through its prayer meetings: come, Holy Spirit.

how: Catholics in the charismatic renewal gather in prayer groups, often in parish halls, for songs of praise, scripture, spontaneous prayer and sometimes praying in tongues, and they pray for a renewal of the Holy Spirit's gifts first given in baptism and confirmation. Other Catholics take no part, and both are fully part of the Church.

o: a Catholic movement of praise, asking for the Spirit's gifts
a new sacrament some Catholics receive after confirmation
a breakaway church that left Rome over speaking in tongues

games.q: you're one of the students on that retreat. it's Saturday night, and you've been reading about Pentecost all weekend. what do the students do, by the movement's own telling?
o: wander into the chapel one by one and stay a long time, praying and praising.
write a rule for a new religious order.
games.why: by the movement's own telling, they drifted into the chapel one by one and stayed, praying and praising. nobody had planned it.

practice: Praise is different from asking and from thanks: it names what someone is, not what they've done for you.
If you pray, praise God in your own plain words, one name or one quality at a time, beginning the way the renewal does: come, Holy Spirit.
If you don't, name things that are good simply because they are: light, a voice you love, water.

wordCard.voice: Charismatic renewal. A Catholic movement of praise that asks the Holy Spirit to stir up the gifts of grace Paul called charisms. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, a gift of grace: Paul's word in his letter to Corinth.
